Pregnancy

Cordia myxa in pregnancy: fruit, traditional uses and safety

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Cordia myxa, also called sepestan or Assyrian plum, is used as food and in traditional remedies. Those uses do not establish a pregnancy benefit or a safe medicinal dose. The useful distinction is between an identified food fruit and a particular leaf, bark, syrup or extract: not between ‘natural’ and ‘chemical’.

Which plant and preparation do you have?

Kew accepts the name Cordia myxa L. in the Boraginaceae family. It is a tree native from southern Iran towards Indo-China and cultivated more widely in Asia and Africa. Broad leaves and white or cream flowers accompany small rounded or oval stone fruits. Descriptions include yellow, apricot, pinkish or dark fruit with a persistent cup-like calyx and sweet, sticky flesh; appearance varies.

A description or photograph cannot authenticate a product. Common names and closely related plants can be confused. Fresh or dried edible fruit, sweetened syrup, medicinal tea, leaf or bark material and concentrated extracts are different exposures. Ask for the botanical name, part used and full ingredients; do not forage an unidentified plant.

Chemical findings are not pregnancy treatment evidence

Researchers have studied plant compounds, including flavonoids and other phenolics, using fruit and leaf extracts. Antioxidant and enzyme effects in laboratory tests do not show that eating the fruit improves a pregnancy or treats disease. An extraction solvent such as ethanol describes how a research preparation was made; an ‘alcoholic extract’ is not a nutrient naturally supplied by the fruit.

A familiar food, a concentrated extract and a mixed herbal medicine cannot share a single safety conclusion. Strength, plant part, added ingredients and manufacturing quality matter. Do not replace recommended pregnancy supplements or prescribed treatment with a list of plant chemicals.

Cough, hoarseness, fever and pain claims

Traditional uses include cough, chest irritation, hoarseness, bringing up mucus, dry mouth, thirst, fever, stomach discomfort and rheumatic pain. Cordia fruit extracts have been tested for cough and pain in mice. These experiments do not establish symptom relief, a home dose or fetal safety in pregnant people. ‘Anti-inflammatory’ and ‘antioxidant’ are not guarantees of clinical benefit.

For a mild cold, rest and adequate fluids may help comfort. Ask a pharmacist about pregnancy-appropriate symptom treatment; paracetamol may be suitable for pain or fever when used as advised. Suspected flu, persistent fever, worsening cough or feeling increasingly unwell needs clinical advice. Do not delay care while trying a syrup or assume that expectorant claims treat the cause.

Digestive, kidney and external uses need separate assessment

A small single-centre trial reported improvement with a particular Cordia syrup in children with gastroenteritis. It studied children, not pregnancy, and had short follow-up. It does not establish treatment for pregnancy stomach pain, diarrhoea or kidney disease, and is not a recipe for a homemade syrup. Claims about diuresis or ‘blood purification’ do not justify treating infection or changing body fluids yourself.

Leaf or bark preparations and poultices for headache or wounds are different from fruit food use. There is no established pregnancy benefit for these home treatments. Do not put unsterile plant material on an open wound or in an eye. Burning urine or suspected UTI in pregnancy needs urgent same-day assessment; fever or pain in the back below the ribs makes prompt assessment particularly important.

Is it safe to eat during pregnancy?

The sources reviewed do not establish reliable human pregnancy-outcome data for Cordia myxa or a validated safe amount, trimester or medicinal preparation. Do not start a strong tea, extract, leaf or bark remedy yourself. Ask your maternity clinician or pharmacist about the exact product and why you want to use it. Lack of data proves neither safety nor inevitable harm.

Ordinary food use differs from medicinal treatment, but a history of eating a fruit does not establish a pregnancy-specific safe dose. You can choose another familiar fruit. If discussing food use, check identity and preparation, wash produce under running water without soap or bleach, and follow food-storage instructions. Washing or cooking does not turn an uncertain medicinal product into a proven safe one.

What about side effects, glucose and ‘coldness’?

Digestive discomfort or an allergic reaction is possible after food or herbal products, but the pregnancy risks and frequency of Cordia-specific reactions are not well defined. The evidence reviewed does not establish that an ordinary serving predictably damages the stomach or liver or raises blood glucose. It also does not justify promising that serious effects cannot occur.

Fruit and sweetened syrups contain carbohydrate; added sugar and portions matter, particularly with gestational diabetes. Follow your agreed food and glucose-monitoring plan, not claims that Cordia either cures diabetes or inevitably worsens it. ‘Coldness’ in a traditional humour system is not an established biomedical adverse effect. Do not use another herb or stop prescribed medicines to counteract it.

If you already ate fruit or used a remedy

Record the name, ingredients, plant part, preparation, amount, timing, pregnancy stage and any symptoms. Keep the label or packaging and ask for an individual assessment, especially for a concentrated, mixed or unidentified product. An exposure alone does not diagnose miscarriage or fetal injury or automatically determine extra tests. Necessary prescribed treatment should continue unless your clinician changes it.

Possible poisoning needs immediate medical or poison-service advice; do not wait for symptoms. Do not induce vomiting or give food or drink while awaiting poisoning advice. Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or concerning abdominal symptoms need clinical assessment rather than an assumed food explanation. Suspected UTI with confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking needs emergency help.

Which symptoms should not wait?

Contact maternity or early-pregnancy care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, even spotting. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, needs emergency assessment. Pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion is also an emergency. Heavy pregnancy bleeding alone, or bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness or dizziness, needs emergency care.

Sudden mouth, tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, or a suspected severe allergic reaction needs emergency help even without a rash. Use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector as directed and call emergency services. Do not drive yourself in an emergency; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not wait for a herb to work or an app to assess the symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Show your pharmacist or maternity clinician the species, plant part, label and medicines before using a medicinal preparation.

Ask for a symptom-specific plan for cough, fever, pain or urinary symptoms; do not substitute a syrup or a detox claim for assessment.

Record any exposure and symptoms, keep the packaging and use urgent or emergency care for the warning signs described.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise product details, amounts, timing, symptoms and questions for your care team. It cannot identify a plant, certify pregnancy safety, choose a medicinal dose, diagnose toxicity or assess fetal wellbeing. Records must not delay care.

When to seek help

Pregnancy benefit and a safe medicinal dose are not established. Do not self-treat. Any pregnancy bleeding needs immediate maternity advice. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment. Sudden mouth or airway swelling or a suspected severe allergy also needs emergency help. Do not drive yourself. Suspected UTI in pregnancy needs urgent same-day care; confusion, drowsiness or speech difficulty needs emergency help. Possible poisoning needs immediate advice; do not induce vomiting or give food or drink while waiting.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Confirm the species, plant part and preparation; a fruit picture cannot authenticate a product.
  • Traditional uses and laboratory or animal findings do not establish pregnancy benefit or a medicinal dose.
  • A childhood syrup trial cannot prove pregnancy safety or justify a home recipe.
  • Keep food and glucose decisions separate from unproven kidney, liver, detoxification or ‘coldness’ claims.
  • After exposure, share details without assuming harm; pregnancy, allergy and poisoning warnings need appropriate care.

Frequently asked questions

What benefits are proven during pregnancy?

The evidence reviewed does not establish Cordia myxa as a pregnancy treatment for cough, fever, pain, digestive or kidney problems. Traditional use and laboratory findings are different from demonstrated benefit in pregnant people.

Is Cordia myxa safe during pregnancy?

Reliable pregnancy-outcome data and a safe medicinal dose are not established here. Food fruit and concentrated products differ. Have the exact product reviewed before medicinal use; uncertainty is not proof of safety or harm.

What side effects can it cause?

Digestive symptoms or allergy are possible, but Cordia-specific pregnancy risks and their frequency are poorly defined. Claims of predictable liver injury, glucose rise or biomedical ‘coldness’ are not established by the evidence reviewed. Concerning symptoms need assessment.

Should I eat it while pregnant?

You do not need this fruit or a remedy made from it for a healthy pregnancy. You may choose another familiar fruit. Discuss identity, preparation, your health and medicines with your care team rather than following an unsupported fruit count or dose.

Does the children’s syrup trial prove it works for me?

No. A particular syrup was studied for childhood gastroenteritis with short follow-up. That does not establish benefit for pregnancy symptoms, safety for a fetus or an equivalent homemade preparation.

Can I use the leaves, bark or a strong tea instead?

Do not assume these are equivalent to food fruit. Plant part, extraction, strength and other ingredients change the exposure. Ask a pharmacist or maternity clinician before use, and do not put unsterile plant material on wounds or in eyes.

I already took some: what should I do?

Keep product details, amount and timing and ask for individual advice without assuming fetal harm. Possible poisoning needs immediate advice; do not induce vomiting or give food or drink while waiting. Keep necessary prescribed treatment unless your clinician changes it.

When do I need urgent or emergency help?

Any pregnancy bleeding needs immediate maternity advice. Severe or worsening pelvic pain or pain with movement or touch, heavy bleeding, pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain or breathing difficulty, or a serious allergic reaction needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Suspected UTI in pregnancy needs urgent same-day assessment; confusion, drowsiness or speech difficulty needs emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
